worklist.title: ACT TO IMPROVE RURAL MAIL SERVICE / Plan To Bring City Delivery For Residents In North Section Of Parma Township / Interested in bringing about better mail service throughout the entire Brooklyn community, President Ira D. Siegfried, of the Southwestern Civic and Business Men's Association, has selected a committee to take up the matter with the postal authorities. / The committee already has started to work and has made interesting progress. To get city delivery for most of Parma Township between Pearl and State roads, north of Snow road, is the aim of the association, and according to the superintendent of the Brooklyn post office station, such a step would eliminate much of the mail irregularity on the rural route on State road. However, before city delivery can be furnished, the streets must be supplied with sidewalks and the houses must be numbered. The Southwestern Association is working vigorously to bring these improvements about. / The population in the northern part of Parma Township is so large that rural service is no longer practical, says the Brooklyn postal superintendent, adding, however, that much of the complaints arising now in the rural section from slow delivery of mail is due to improper addressing or failure of new residents on the rural routes to notify the Brooklyn postal station of their location.
worklist.summary: A Brooklyn community group is pushing postal officials to switch part of Parma Township from rural to city mail delivery, though sidewalks and house numbering must come first.
worklist.contextHint: Reflects the 1920s transition of growing suburban townships from rural free delivery to city-style postal service as population density increased.

worklist.summary: An editorial defends the Bok peace plan against skeptics, urging readers to read it themselves before judging.
worklist.contextHint: Refers to the widely publicized Bok Peace Award of 1923-24, a contest sponsored by editor Edward Bok to find a workable American peace plan.
worklist.transcript:
Vol. X.          Cleveland, Friday, Feb. 1, 1924          No. 5
WHO IS BOK???
'Who is this man Bok, anyway, that he thinks he knows how to draw up a peace plan?'
Would you believe that anyone would ask that question?
It doesn't seem possible, but someone did. In fact, more than one person did and those who ask were intelligent people—leaders of thought in some directions.
Yet the Bok peace plan has been discussed in newspapers and magazines for months. It has been discussed by churches, clubs and organizations of all kinds that are trying to make the world better.
The Bok peace plan may not bring order to a chaotic world. It may not undo in a few months or a few years the evil work of centuries of misunderstanding and hatred, but at least it will serve—and has served—to turn the attention of thinking people into the right channel.
Maybe you will not believe in the Bok peace plan, but there are few normal people who do not believe in peace and welcome any move that will bring it nearer and surer.
At least do not condemn the plan unheard. Get a copy of it and read it. You can get a copy at the Brooklyn Y. M. C. A.

Section 2. That said part which it is hereby declared necessary to construct and maintain in said Cuyahoga County Sewer District 1, Water Supply Improvement 49, the detailed plans, specifications and estimate of cost for which were approved on Jan. 30, 1924 and which improvement is described as follows:
Water mains in Biddulph road from West 75th Street to a point approximately 2400 feet west of West 75th Street; together with all necessary appurtenances.
Section 3. That said Improvement shall be constructed of the materials and in the manner indicated or described on the detailed plans, and in the specifications for said Improvement, which detailed plans and specifications are now on file in the office of the County Sanitary Engineer and open to inspection by all persons interested.
Section 4. That the estimated cost of the said improvement for one year is $1,000.00.
Section 5. That the entire cost of construction and maintenance of said Improvement shall be specially assessed as a local and district assessment against the benefited property in Cuyahoga County Sewer District 1, contained within the following described boundaries:
Beginning at a point in the center line of Ridge Road 1900 feet southerly from the center line of Linndale Road;

TO THE LIVING ABOUT THE DEAD
Three thousand years ago lived an Egyptian King named TUT-ANKH-AMEN. The name sounded like a rattler, so fellow Luxorites called him "Tut" for short.
When "Tut" reached the DANGEROUS AGE, and finally succeeded with his somewhat luxuriant locks, he up and died. Dying was one of the leading indoor sports' then, and "Tut's" death was a Major League event. They proceeded to (w'rap) him as per custom in a series of layers and finally deposited the remains in a tomb in the Valley of Departed Kings.
Three thousand years later, while exploring for a fit spot for "still" development work, dug up "Tut's" tomb with all the medieval relics buried with him. Then the advertising men stepped in and took charge, and in a few weeks gave "Tut" a reputation which shades CHARLIE CHAPLIN, DOUGLAS FAIRBANKS and MARY PICKFORD into oblivion by comparison.
Dead three thousand years! Forgotten! Lost! Then "BANG"—advertised, and the whole world clamored for more news of "Tut."
If advertising can put that much life into something dead for three thousand years, what will it do for a LIVE SUBJECT or PRODUCT? For a LIVE BUSINESS? MY BUSINESS?
They might have dug up a hundred "Tut's," and if they kept the news to themselves, only a few bookworms and historians would have ever heard of it.
Moral: You might have the best product in the world, but unless you TELL them about it, your business will slumber peacefully to death.
And that is why I advertise to you folks in the Brooklyn-Parma community. I want you to know that I have a science that REALLY and ACTUALLY ADJUSTS THE CAUSES of such troubles as paralysis, heart, trouble, diabetes, high blood pressure, tonsilitis, pneumonia, fallen arches, gastritis, tuberculosis, fevers, mumps, deafness and every other affliction you have ever heard of. When you stop to think of it, wouldn't it be about the most suicidal business policy to spend real money on these advertisements if I couldn't make good on what they say. The reason PACKARD, CHICKERING, TIFFANY and VICTROLA spend real money to advertise is because they have the best in the world in their particular line. So have I.
